Hot Stuff: How lifeguards in Port Stanley stay ready to keep beachgoers safe

Meet the unsung heroes of Port Stanley's Main Beach. Part 14 of our series on people and things that make summer sizzle here

Author of the article:
By Allison Young
Published Aug 30, 2026
3 minute read
Join the conversation

Article content

With sun-drenched sand, a sparkling shore and a team of lifeguards keeping beachgoers safe, a day at Port Stanley’s Main Beach could almost pass for an episode of Baywatch. 

Article content
Article content
Article content

But for the Central Elgin Beach Rescue, there’s much more to the job than slow-motion running and dramatic rescues.

Article content

Article content

Lifeguards have been monitoring the nearly 600-metre stretch of Main Beach since their season began in late June. From five towers positioned along the beach, Port Stanley’s lifeguards keep watch as thousands of visitors come each month to enjoy all the beach has to offer, from beach volleyball, strolling the pier and, of course, the refreshing water.

Article content

“We train for the biggest situations and scenarios,” supervising lifeguard Stephen Blankenship said. 

Article content

Main Beach is unique in an area where many beaches are not staffed by lifeguards, including beaches in the same town, like Erie Rest, Little and Pumphouse.

Article content

The first lifeguards at Main Beach were hired in July 1998, after three young men died in separate incidents the previous month. The team at that time consisted of a coordinator, four full-time guards and two part-time guards.

Article content

Nearly three decades later, the team has grown to more than two dozen lifeguards in various roles. Blankenship is one of four supervising lifeguards, with seven summers working on Main Beach and 14 years total of lifeguarding experience. 

Article content
Article content
Article content

As someone who did varsity sports and triathlons, Blankenship said he was drawn to the job for its physicality and team structure.

Article content

Article content

“Working here, you’re going to be a part of a competitive group that has a lot of running, swimming, body weight exercises and then the team aspect of it,” Blankenship said. “We have a great team, so it makes me keep coming back.”

Article content

Another member of that team is senior lifeguard Erica Klosler, who said the job has helped her grow physically, emotionally and mentally. 

Article content

“I definitely learned a lot of discipline, grit and I’m better at working well under pressure. When things go south, I’m good in emergency situations now,” Klosler said.

Article content

Before the lifeguards are back on the beach, they train eight weekends from May to the end of June

Article content

“Even throughout the year, I’m going to the gym and I’m going on a run and I’m doing this for the beach because once you’ve been here enough and you’ve seen what can happen at the beach, it’s really important to be as prepared as you can be,” Klosler said.

Article content

Unlike a pool, Klosler said, the beach is unpredictable. The currents, wind, water conditions and even the people swimming can be very different every time she works. Whether it’s a green-flag day with calm conditions or a red-flag day when the water is more dangerous, the team is always watching for signs that someone needs help.

Article content

Blankenship said the lifeguards do a lot before intervention is necessary, with education and prevention being a major part of their role. That means talking to beachgoers about water safety or helping promote Central Elgin’s Lifejacket Lending Program.

Article content

According to Central Elgin officials, the lifeguards perform about 40 water rescues in a summer, with the most common reason for intervention being people who have gone past their abilities and are not wearing personal flotation devices. 

Article content

“It’s stressful. It’s almost like in those situations, everything except logical thinking takes over,” Klosler said. “In order to respond well, you always need to have a kind of tunnel vision and be like, ‘OK, here’s the next step, here’s the next step.’” 

Article content

Klosler said the team’s support for one another is especially important during and after rescues, knowing they can turn to their teammates for help or to talk through what happened.

Article content

“We formed really good bonds with each other. You almost have to when you’re doing a job like this,” she said. “We trust each other with our lives, literally.”

Article content
Article content

Over the past five summers, Klosler said she has watched the skilled team grow and hopes the community recognizes how important the lifeguards are to a busy beach like Main Beach. “I think it’s really important for everybody to be able to come and enjoy the beach and the water and everybody to go home safely.”

      I don't believe that you have the start date correct for the lifeguards at Port. It started after two Grand Bend Lifeguards pushed the town to reduce unnecessary drowning. There was a coroner's inquest in or around 1982 and the beach patrol followed a year or so later. It's great that the lifeguards have continued to be funded. It's also great that the beach is now posted with information on rip tides. Grand Bend and Port Stanley differ in this regard. Grand Bend is more of an undertow and Port has more rips. Great story.
